approach: Frame-prediction AE; spatial-rotation and temporal-mixing patch transforms applied only in training, so inference is a plain small AE
protocol_notes: Frame-level AUC, aggregation not labelled. Per Eq. 7, PSNR is min-max normalized 'of each video clip to the range [0, 1]', which is a per-video test-time statistic. FPS covers frame generation plus scoring on the Ped2 test set. Inference batch size and data loading are not stated; batch size 4 is given for training only. Table 1 footnote: starred baseline scores are micro-AUC taken from [9, 11]; baseline FPS marked with a dagger were re-implemented on the same device, the rest were copied from the papers.
hardware: Desktop GPU: single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090
supervision_evidence: Sec. 3.1/3.2: 'we apply our patch anomaly generation to the frame cuboid'. SRT (random 0/90/180/270 patch rotation) and TMT (temporal shuffling of a 60x60 patch cuboid) generate abnormal appearance and motion in normal training frames. Related work: 'transform the input frames ... to generate abnormal frames within training datasets'. Not used at inference.
lookahead_frames: 0 (5 past frames predict the next frame), but the per-clip min-max uses the max/min PSNR of the whole test video
notes: CONFIRMED (borderline). The pseudo-anomalies are made only from the target's own normal frames, with no external data and no anomaly labels or classifier. The training target is the real next frame (input-side corruption, like Astrid et al. LNTRA), and the paper itself calls the setting 'unsupervised' with normal-only training data. The class follows the task definition ('pseudo-anomaly generation') and the authors' own wording. If the table instead separates by data source (external or real anomalies vs. target-normal only), this row and HSC move to one-class, and SSMTL/SSMTL++v2 stay there. Eq. 7: PSNR is min-max normalised 'of each video clip to the range [0, 1]'. No temporal smoothing is stated. The only stated per-dataset difference is training epochs (20 for Avenue/Ped2, 5 for ShT); n=5, patch 60x60 and loss weights 0.25/0.75 are shared. The first 5 frames of each clip are excluded from evaluation. AUC aggregation for the own numbers is not labelled; starred baselines are micro.

title: Lightning Fast Video Anomaly Detection via Multi-Scale Adversarial Distillation
authors: Croitoru, Ristea, Dascalescu, Ionescu, Khan, Shah
venue: Computer Vision and Image Understanding, vol. 247, article 104074, Oct 2024
approach: Knowledge distillation: a lightweight frame-level student is distilled, with standard and adversarial losses, from two object-centric (YOLOv3-based) teachers, SSMTL and BA-AED
protocol_notes: Fields are micro AUC. Teachers (with YOLOv3) are used only for training: 'running only the student model at test time'. The student is frame-level, so no detector runs at inference. Whether frame decoding or pre-processing is inside the 1480 FPS is not stated. DOI 10.1016/j.cviu.2024.104074.
hardware: Desktop GPU: written as 'Nvidia GeForce GTX 3090' (24 GB); also CPU Intel i9 3.7 GHz
supervision_evidence: Sec. 3/4.2: teacher T1 = Georgescu et al. (2022b) object-level AEs, T2 = SSMTL (2021), trained with the official code. Sec. 2: Georgescu et al. (2022b) 'extended the framework by introducing pseudo-anomalies during training and attaching classifiers to discriminate between normal and pseudo-abnormal samples'. SSMTL++ Sec. 3.3 identifies that pseudo-anomaly set as external OOD images (flowers, textures, ImageNet).
lookahead_frames: 3 frames (student input is frames i-3, i, i+3 centred on i, temporal step t=3; Fig. 3)
notes: CONFIRMED. The pseudo-anomaly supervision is indirect. The student is pre-trained as an autoencoder, then distilled from frozen-teacher anomaly maps computed on target normal training frames only. Teacher T1 is trained with external OOD pseudo-anomalies; teacher T2 is self-supervised on normal data (plus YOLOv3/ResNet-50 distillation). The adversarial loss is a teacher-vs-student map discriminator, not anomaly supervision. At inference only the frame-level student runs (no detector). The frame score is the mean over the three heads of each head's map maximum. Teacher maps are Gaussian-blurred spatially (training targets only). No temporal smoothing or score normalisation is stated for inference. Per-dataset setting: output head resolutions are 1x1/30x30/60x60 on Ped2 versus 1x1/4x4/16x16 on Avenue/ShT. Alpha=0.1 is set explicitly 'without tuning'. However, the architecture and head-resolution ablations (Sec. 4.5, Tables 5-11) report test-set AUC and were used for design choices ('When making our design choices, we refer to the micro AUC'). Micro and macro AUC are both reported; the listed values are micro.

title: Anomaly Detection in Video via Self-Supervised and Multi-Task Learning (SSMTL)
authors: Georgescu, Barbalau, Ionescu, Khan, Popescu, Shah
approach: Object-centric: YOLOv3 detections, then a lightweight 3D CNN trained jointly on three self-supervised proxy tasks plus knowledge distillation (four tasks in total)
protocol_notes: The paper reports one frame-level AUC per dataset without naming the aggregation. SD-MAE (CVPR'24) Table 1 lists SSMTL as micro 91.5 / 82.4 / 97.5 and macro 92.8 / 90.2 / 99.8 (Avenue / SHT / Ped2), so the paper's own figures match the macro values. SD-MAE lists SSMTL at 51 FPS, re-timed on its GTX 3090. Per Sec 6.2 the 23/21 FPS includes the YOLOv3 detector.
hardware: Desktop GPU: single GeForce GTX 1080Ti 11 GB
supervision_evidence: Sec. 4.1: 'Each data set has pre-defined training and test sets, anomalous events being included only at test time'. Sec. 3: a 3D CNN is trained on self-supervised proxy tasks (arrow of time, motion irregularity, middle-box prediction) plus distillation from pretrained YOLOv3/ResNet-50. The same group later states that Georgescu et al. (2022b) 'extended the framework by introducing pseudo-anomalies', which implies SSMTL itself has none.
lookahead_frames: 3 frames from the object-centric sequence {i-3..i+3} (t=3), plus a 3D mean filter and a temporal Gaussian filter (sigma not stated)
notes: CONFIRMED (borderline class). The listed values (Avenue 92.8 / ShT 90.2 / Ped2 99.8) are the late fusion of the object-level and frame-level frameworks (Table 2), so granularity is hybrid. Object-level alone gives 91.9 / 89.3 / 99.8. The ShT 90.2 is the standard one-class split, not the weakly supervised split. It is a macro-style AUC: SD-MAE re-lists it as macro (micro 82.4), and the same group's SSMTL++ Tables 7/8 list SSMTL as Avenue micro 91.5 / macro 91.9 and ShT micro 82.4 / macro 89.3, matching this paper's object-level figures. So it is not comparable with micro numbers. Borderline class: T2 trains a classifier to separate regular from frame-skipped ('intermittent') sequences built from normal data, and P(intermittent) is used as an anomaly score. That is functionally the skip-frame pseudo-anomaly of Astrid et al., but the authors frame it as a self-supervised proxy task. No external data or real anomalies are used. Keep one-class unless the table adopts a strict 'any self-generated abnormal samples' rule, which would also move SSMTL++v2. Paper Sec. 3.4: 3D mean filter on the anomaly map, frame score = max, then 'applying a temporal Gaussian filter'. Per-dataset settings: lambda=0.5 for Ped2 vs 0.2 for Avenue/ShT, and detection confidence 0.5 for Ped2 vs 0.8. Lambda and t are tuned on a 15% validation split of the training videos (proxy-task loss), not on test.

title: M2S2L: Mamba-based Multi-Scale Spatial-temporal Learning for Video Anomaly Detection
authors: Liu, Chen, Zhu, Liu, Sun, Zhou

title: Unsupervised Video Anomaly Detection Using Video Vision Transformer and Adversarial Training
approach: ViViT encoder generator predicting future frame and optical-flow magnitude (Farneback), with U-Net discriminator (adversarial)
protocol_notes: Scores are normalized by the maximum over each test video, a test-time statistic. Micro or macro aggregation is not stated. SHT 85.8 is unusually high for a frame-prediction model. DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2025.3554813.
hardware: Workstation: i7-9700X + RTX 2080 Ti (development; no timing reported)
supervision_evidence: Sec. III-D: 'The proposed network is trained only on normal videos, allowing it to accurately predict normal events.' Sec. II: ShanghaiTech is '330 training videos without abnormal events and 107 testing videos'.
lookahead_frames: 0 for the raw a(t), since four consecutive past frames predict the frame and its flow magnitude. The Eq. (12) normalisation S(t) = a(t) / max(a(1..T)) is 'computed over all frames T in the test video', so the final score depends on the whole test video, future frames included.
notes: CONFIRMED. I re-read the full text. A ViViT generator predicts the future frame and the Farneback flow magnitude. Feature differences from the U-Net discriminator weight the score (Eq. 11). Per-video max normalisation is a non-causal statistic computed at test time. Only one hyperparameter set is reported (batch 1, 30 epochs, LR 1e-4/1e-5, lambda_I=200, lambda_O=100), not split by dataset. The SHT test set is described as 23,465 normal + 17,326 abnormal = 40,791 frames, the standard one-class split rather than the weakly supervised split, so 85.8 is not a weakly supervised split number. Micro or macro AUC is not stated. Datasets are Ped2 and SHT only.

title: Attention-Enhanced and Quantization-Aware GRU-DCGAN for Efficient Surveillance Video Abnormal Behavior Detection
approach: GRU-DCGAN with spatial + temporal attention and 8-bit quantization-aware training; discriminator scores frames
protocol_notes: Datasets come from SVIP Lab and Kaggle, with frames re-extracted at 25 fps. The Ped2 test set is reported as 4,020 frames, while the standard set is 2,010. The paper also reports threshold-based accuracy and F1. Ped2 AUC (84.39) is far below the usual unsupervised range, yet SHT is higher. Table 8 compares against GPU methods (45-127 FPS on GPU).
hardware: CPU only: Intel Xeon Gold 6248 2.5 GHz server (TensorFlow/Keras, Windows Server 2016)
supervision_evidence: Algorithm 1 trains the GAN adversarially on 'real sequences x1:T ~ pdata(x)' from the training split, with no anomaly labels (Eqs. 25-27: the discriminator separates real from generated sequences). Sec. IV-D training frame counts are 2,550 (Ped2), 15,328 (Avenue) and 274,515 (SHT), which equal the standard normal-only training splits. Eq. (32): the anomaly score is the discriminator's normality output S(x).
lookahead_frames: not_stated. Eq. (11) (GRU in the discriminator) is causal within a sequence, but inputs are 14-frame sequences and D outputs one value per sequence, D(X1:T) in Eq. 25. How sequence outputs map to per-frame scores is not given. If a sequence score is assigned to all of its frames, the lookahead is up to 13.
notes: CORRECTED: two changes. (1) lookahead changed from '0' to not_stated, because the discriminator scores 14-frame sequences (Eq. 25) and the mapping from sequence to frame is not described, so 0 was not supported. (2) The earlier note said the SHT test set (42,883 frames) is non-standard. That is wrong: 274,515 + 42,883 = 317,398 is the official ShanghaiTech frame count, and other papers in this list (for example SPARTA) quote 42,883 too, while 40,791 is the frame-label total. Only Ped2 is off: 4,020 test frames against the official 2,010, and 6,570 total against the official 4,560. Ped1 is also inflated (22,800 against 14,000). Avenue matches the official counts. Everything else is unchanged. The paper never says 'trained only on normal data' in so many words. The one-class label rests on unlabelled adversarial training plus the standard training-split sizes. Data come from SVIP Lab and Kaggle, re-extracted at 25 fps. Hyperparameters come from prior work [17], and Table 2 is an image. The QAT bit-width was chosen on Avenue (Table 1). The Youden-J threshold is used for accuracy/F1, not for AUC. Inference is CPU-only.

title: Human-Centric Video Anomaly Detection Through Spatio-Temporal Pose Tokenization and Transformer (SPARTA)
approach: Pose-based transformer: ST-PRP pose and relative-pose tokenization, unified encoder with twin (current/future) decoders
protocol_notes: Pose comes from AlphaPose (SHT); whether the 5.96 ms includes pose estimation is unclear. Frame score is the maximum over individuals. No Ped2 or Avenue.
hardware: Inference hardware not stated; training on 3x RTX A6000 + AMD EPYC 7513
supervision_evidence: Sec. III: 'The learning problem is formulated as self-supervised one-class anomaly detection'. Sec. III-B: the CTD is trained 'on the normal data samples in the training set'. Sec. IV-D: 'The training approach is entirely self-supervised, identifying the best model through the minimization of MSE loss on the training data. This model is then subjected to a single evaluation on the test set'.
lookahead_frames: 11 on SHT (beta/2 - 1 with beta = 24). CTD reconstructs the window t0..t0+beta-1, and FTD predicts the same window from t0-beta..t0-1. Both errors are computed on the window t0..t0+beta-1 and assigned to frame t0+beta/2 (Eqs. 6, 7, 10, 11), so frames up to t0+beta-1 = t+11 are used.
notes: CONFIRMED. I re-read the full IEEE text. Poses come from pretrained AlphaPose with tracking on SHT. The person score is 0.5*Norm(CS) + 0.5*Norm(FS), and the frame score is the maximum over persons. The type and scope of Norm() are not stated. A 'conventional grid hyper-parameter search' was used, with ranges and criterion in the supplementary material. Window length, learning rate and epochs differ per dataset (SHT: beta=24, CTD 20 epochs at 1e-5, FTD 30 epochs at 2e-3; CHAD beta=30; NWPUC beta=24 with other LRs). The paper does not say whether the 5.96 ms latency includes pose estimation. No Ped2 or Avenue results. The SHT number (85.75) is on the standard one-class split, not the weakly supervised one, and the paper cites 274,515 training and 42,883 test frames.

title: Confidence-Aware Cascaded Learning for Real-Time Weakly Supervised Anomaly Detection in Surveillance Video (CASRE)
approach: Cascade: temperature-scaled ResNet3D primary classifier; low-confidence clips (<6%) routed to MViTv2 fallback; calibrated fusion
protocol_notes: PROTOCOL BREAK: clip-level (50-frame) binary classification with clip-level weak supervision. Normal clips from test sequences were added to training, and the Ped2 test set has only 14 clips. This is not frame-level AUC, so Ped2 is left null.
hardware: Desktop: i9-9900K + RTX 2080 Ti
supervision_evidence: Sec. IV-A.3 (UCSD): 'each video is segmented into fixed-length temporal clips of L = 50 frames using annotation-guided temporal partitioning ... ensuring temporal coherence and label consistency', and 'the annotated test sequences yield up to 96 anomalous clips'. For Ped2, 'additional normal clips(11) from test normal intervals are incorporated', giving '30 normal and 30 anomalous clips for training, and 7 normal and 7 anomalous clips for testing'. Sec. IV-D: 'trained as binary classifiers (normal vs. anomalous)'.
lookahead_frames: Not applicable: the method scores whole 50-frame clips (built from 300-frame segments at 5 fps on UCF-Crime and annotation-guided 50-frame partitions on UCSD) and produces no frame-level score.
notes: CONFIRMED. I re-read the full text. The paper calls itself 'clip-level weak supervision (CLWS)', and on UCF-Crime clip labels are 'inherited from the parent video annotation', which is weak. On UCSD, however, the frame-level ground truth drives the partitioning, so each training clip is label-homogeneous. That makes it supervised trimmed-clip classification, and fully_supervised applies in the Ped2/Avenue/SHT setting. The anomalous training clips have to come from the test videos, since Ped2 training videos contain no anomalies, and the test set has only 7+7 Ped2 clips. Metrics are clip-level accuracy and AUC (macro OvR in the multi-class case), not frame-level AUC. tau = 0.5 and the hyperparameters in Tables 4-5 are shared across datasets, with 50 epochs for all. Per-video normalisation is set to 'no' because the outputs are calibrated softmax probabilities and the paper describes no per-video rescaling. Not comparable to one-class Ped2/Avenue/SHT results.
